title: Quantum Optomechanics with Imperfect Mirrors and Casimir-Polder Effect of Atoms with Different Dynamic Polarizabilities: A Unified Treatment via a Microscopic Model
abstract: This work aims at bringing the microphysics model of quantum optomechanics (QOM) proposed in [1] and developed in [2, 3] one step closer to be applicable to realistic experimental conditions, specifically, for imperfect mirrors, and for real materials. The atom/mirror-oscillator-field (AMOF) model features an internal degree of freedom for a mirror or an atom whose interaction with a quantum field determines the transmission functions of a mirror or the dynamic polarizability of an atom. We study three problems with this model: 1) An imperfect mirror moving in a cavity field, comparing results from the AMOF model with the boundary condition methods; 2) We analyze how well the dynamic polarizability derived from the AMOF model fits the tabulated data at different frequencies. 3) Combining these two parts we analyze the quantum fluctuations induced Casimir-Polder energy between a dilute atom space and a wall. We examine how well we can use the three constituent parameters of the idf oscillator in the AMOF model to match with published results on a meta-stable He* atom near a Au plate and found excellent agreements. These examples show that the AMOF model not only has a sound theoretical structure, because it is based on the microphysics dynamics of the basic constituents, it also has good practical values because it can produce accurate results for certain real materials.
summary: This paper develops the Atom/Mirror-Oscillator-Field (AMOF) model, a microscopic theory for quantum optomechanics. It demonstrates the model's versatility by successfully calculating phenomena ranging from cavity field interactions with imperfect mirrors to the Casimir-Polder force between atoms and surfaces. The key contribution is showing that a single, unified microscopic framework can accurately describe diverse quantum optical and material physics problems.
main_problem: The work aims to create a unified, microscopic model for quantum optomechanics (QOM) that accurately describes interactions involving imperfect mirrors and atoms with complex dynamic polarizabilities.
main_result: The proposed Atom/Mirror-Oscillator-Field (AMOF) model successfully reproduces established results for both cavity optomechanics (e.g., particle creation) and the Casimir-Polder force, showing excellent agreement with real material data.
method: The authors employ a microscopic Hamiltonian approach, integrating out the internal oscillator degrees of freedom to derive effective field theories for calculating observables like transmission functions and free energy.
model_or_system: The core is the AMOF model, which extends the MOF model by incorporating an internal degree of freedom (idf) for atoms or mirrors. This model describes the interaction between a quantum field ($\Phi$) and the mechanical/internal oscillator modes, allowing for a unified treatment of different physical boundaries.
key_observables: Transmission/reflection functions ($R(\omega), T(\omega)$), quantum fluctuations (particle number $N_{	ext{out}}(\omega)$), and the Casimir-Polder free energy ($F_A$).
important_parameters: The three intrinsic constituent parameters of the idf oscillator ($\lambda, m, \Omega$), and material properties like plasma frequencies or coupling strengths.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations such as the small displacement limit for mirrors and the dilute atomic limit for the Casimir-Polder calculation.

paper_structure: The paper systematically tackles three related problems: 1) Imperfect mirrors in a cavity field, 2) Fitting the model's dynamic polarizability to tabulated data, and 3) Combining these to analyze the quantum-fluctuation-induced Casimir-Polder energy.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a rigorous, first-principles framework (microscopic dynamics) to calculate phenomena in open quantum systems, bridging the gap between idealized theoretical models and complex, real-world experimental setups in quantum optics and AMO.
